prompt: What did Richard Oldham's 1906 paper establish?
options: That the Earth has a central core
That the core is liquid
That the inner core is solid
That the crust is about 50 km thick under continents
correctAnswer: That the Earth has a central core
explanation: Oldham showed that P-waves reaching the far side of the Earth arrive late, so they must cross a central core where they travel more slowly. He thought the core was dense and probably iron, not liquid.

prompt: Oldham showed that the Earth's core is liquid.
explanation: Oldham established that a core exists, but he explained its slowness with a very dense, probably iron core. The liquid core came later, from Jeffreys's 1926 rigidity argument.

prompt: Jeffreys compared the rigidity of the mantle, measured by seismic waves, with the rigidity of the whole Earth, measured by the _____ raised in the solid Earth by the Moon and Sun.
acceptableAnswers: tidal flexing of the solid Earth
explanation: Tidal flexing measures the rigidity of the planet as a whole. Because the mantle is much more rigid than that average, something below it must have very low rigidity: a liquid core.

prompt: Match each seismologist to the contribution:

pairs.right: Late P-waves reveal a slow central core
Core–mantle boundary at about 2,900 km
Rigidity argument for a liquid core
An inner core from P-waves in the shadow zone

explanation: Oldham found the core (1906), Gutenberg measured its depth, Jeffreys showed it is liquid (1926) and Lehmann proposed the inner core in her 1936 paper P′.

prompt: Why can S-waves not cross the liquid outer core?
options: A liquid has zero shear modulus, so it cannot carry shear waves
The outer core is too hot for any wave to travel through
S-waves are absorbed by the magnetic field
S-waves fade away before they reach the core
correctAnswer: A liquid has zero shear modulus, so it cannot carry shear waves
explanation: S-wave speed depends only on the shear modulus μ and density. In a liquid μ = 0, so no S-waves pass, which leaves an S-wave shadow on the far side of the Earth. P-waves still cross, because they also depend on the bulk modulus.

prompt: The key anomaly in Lehmann's study of the 1929 Buller earthquake was strong P-wave arrivals at stations inside the shadow zone.
explanation: Two stations squarely inside the shadow zone recorded unusually large P-wave amplitudes. A core liquid all the way through could not explain them; a faster inner core that refracts waves into the shadow could.

prompt: Find the error in this reconstruction of Jeffreys's argument:
steps: Tidal flexing of the solid Earth measures the rigidity of the planet as a whole.
Seismic waves measure the rigidity of the mantle.
The mantle turns out to be much less rigid than the Earth as a whole.
So a region below the mantle must make up the difference.
That region, the core, has very low rigidity and must be liquid.
explanation: Step 3 is reversed. Jeffreys showed that the mantle is much more rigid than the Earth as a whole, so a region below it must be far less rigid to bring the average down. That region is the liquid core.

prompt: Lehmann's 1936 analysis showed that a faster inner region exists. What remained unproven until the early 1970s?
options: That the inner core is solid
That an inner core exists at all
That the outer core is liquid
The depth of the core–mantle boundary
correctAnswer: That the inner core is solid
explanation: Faster waves explain the arrivals in the shadow zone, but they do not by themselves show the inner region is solid. Solidity was settled in the early 1970s using the Earth's free oscillations.

prompt: What does seismic tomography map?
options: Departures of seismic wave speed from a one-dimensional reference model
The exact temperature at every point in the mantle
The chemical composition of the crust alone
The magnitudes of past earthquakes
correctAnswer: Departures of seismic wave speed from a one-dimensional reference model
explanation: Tomography inverts travel-time residuals, the differences between observed arrivals and those predicted by a reference model such as PREM, to map three-dimensional speed anomalies. Temperature, composition and melt must then be inferred.

prompt: Away from the top and bottom of the mantle, lateral variations in seismic wave speed are typically tens of per cent.
explanation: They do not exceed a few per cent, except in the uppermost and lowermost mantle. Depth dominates: speeds rise by about 70% from the Moho to the core–mantle boundary.

prompt: The best-known one-dimensional reference model of the Earth, published by Dziewoński and Anderson in 1981, is known by the acronym _____.
explanation: The Preliminary Reference Earth Model was built from seismic travel times, free-oscillation frequencies and astrometric data. Tomography maps departures from models like it.

prompt: Match each group of slabs to how tomography sees it:

pairs.right: Lie flat above the 660 km boundary
Have crossed the 660 km boundary
Stall above about 1,000 km depth
Remains seen at 1,500 and 2,800 km depth

explanation: Slabs behave differently at 660 km, where an endothermic phase change and a viscosity increase resist them. Fukao and Obayashi added a group stalled near 1,000 km, and the oldest slabs form a graveyard deep in the lower mantle.

prompt: Why do travel-time models built from distant earthquakes struggle to locate the depth of anomalies in the upper mantle?
options: The waves travel nearly vertically through the upper mantle
The upper mantle is liquid
No earthquakes occur in the upper mantle
Upper-mantle anomalies are too large to image
correctAnswer: The waves travel nearly vertically through the upper mantle
explanation: A near-vertical ray accumulates delay along a column, so it cannot say at what depth within the top 700–1,000 km the anomaly lies. Crossing paths at other angles are needed.

prompt: If a checkerboard test recovers its pattern well, a tomographic model can be trusted at every scale.
explanation: A checkerboard represents only a single wavelength of heterogeneity, so good recovery says little about other scales. Such tests can mislead, which is why agreement between independent models matters.

prompt: Put the steps of a tomographic study in order:
steps: Record arrival times of seismic waves at many stations
Predict the arrival times in a one-dimensional reference model such as PREM
Form travel-time residuals: observed minus predicted
Invert many crossing paths, with regularisation, for 3D speed anomalies
Test the resolution with synthetic patterns such as checkerboards
explanation: Residuals relative to a reference model are inverted for anomalies; regularisation stabilises the answer, and synthetic tests check which features the ray coverage can actually resolve.

prompt: Why can a narrow, purely thermal plume in the lower mantle be missed by tomography?
options: It barely disturbs passing waves and the wavefront heals, giving delays of less than a second
It is faster than the surrounding mantle, so it looks like a slab
Plumes exist only in the upper mantle
Seismometers cannot record waves that pass through hot rock
correctAnswer: It barely disturbs passing waves and the wavefront heals, giving delays of less than a second
explanation: Diffraction lets a wavefront heal after passing a thin slow feature, so the expected delays are tiny. A thin plume tail can vanish or be smeared into something broader.

prompt: Which mineral did Pearson and colleagues find inside a diamond from Juína, Brazil, in 2014?
options: Ringwoodite
Post-perovskite
Quartz
Olivine
explanation: It was the first higher-pressure form of olivine found in a rock from Earth, and its water content showed that the transition zone is hydrous, at least locally.

prompt: Ringwoodite can hold far more water than the bridgmanite that forms below 660 km.
explanation: Ringwoodite and wadsleyite can hold water up to around 2.5% of their weight, but bridgmanite can hold almost none. That contrast is what drives dehydration melting at 660 km.

prompt: Melting that occurs when water-rich ringwoodite is carried below 660 km and turns into minerals that cannot hold the water is called _____ melting.
explanation: Schmandt and Jacobsen found seismic evidence for this dehydration melting just below 660 km beneath North America, where mantle appears to be flowing down.

prompt: Match each depth to the change in olivine's structure:

pairs.right: Olivine becomes wadsleyite
Wadsleyite becomes ringwoodite
Ringwoodite breaks down into bridgmanite and ferropericlase

explanation: These solid-state phase changes, not changes of rock type, cause the jumps in seismic speed that bound and divide the mantle transition zone.

prompt: Why is the 660 km boundary pushed deeper inside a cold sinking slab?
options: The transition is endothermic, with a negative Clapeyron slope
The transition is exothermic, with a positive Clapeyron slope
Cold rock is less dense than hot rock
Slabs are made of a different mineral from the mantle
correctAnswer: The transition is endothermic, with a negative Clapeyron slope
explanation: With a negative slope, colder rock transforms at higher pressure, so the boundary sits deeper in the slab. The slab stays in the lighter ringwoodite form longer, which resists its descent.

prompt: The Juína diamond showed that the whole transition zone contains about 1% water by weight.
explanation: The diamond showed the transition zone is hydrous to about 1% by weight at least locally. One inclusion cannot reveal the global average, and other evidence points to variable hydration.

prompt: Find the error in this account of dehydration melting:
steps: Water-bearing ringwoodite is carried down out of the transition zone by sinking flow.
Below 660 km it transforms into bridgmanite and (Mg,Fe)O.
Bridgmanite can store even more water than ringwoodite, so the water stays locked in the crystals.
The released water causes a little melting just below 660 km.
The melt lowers seismic wave speeds, which USArray detected.
explanation: Step 3 is wrong: bridgmanite can hold almost no water. The water is forced out, a little of the rock melts, and the melt slows seismic waves just below 660 km.

prompt: In a cold sinking slab, how do the 410 km and 660 km boundaries behave?
options: The 410 bulges upward while the 660 is pushed deeper
Both are pushed deeper
Both bulge upward
The 410 is pushed deeper while the 660 bulges upward
correctAnswer: The 410 bulges upward while the 660 is pushed deeper
explanation: The 410 transition is exothermic with a positive Clapeyron slope, so cold rock transforms at lower pressure; the 660 is endothermic with a negative slope, so cold rock transforms at higher pressure. Their opposite responses make the pair a thermometer.

prompt: Where are the two large low-shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs)?
options: Beneath Africa and the Pacific
Beneath Asia and North America
Beneath the North and South Poles
Beneath the Atlantic and Indian Oceans
explanation: The two provinces, nicknamed Tuzo and Jason, sit on almost exactly opposite sides of the Earth at the base of the mantle.

prompt: Ultra-low velocity zones are thin patches on the core–mantle boundary in which S-wave speeds can drop by up to 30%.
explanation: ULVZs are only tens of kilometres thick, with S-wave reductions of up to 30% and P-wave reductions of up to 10%, far larger than the few per cent of the LLSVPs.

prompt: Above about 125 GPa and 2,500 K, bridgmanite transforms into a denser phase called _____, which may explain the D″ discontinuity.
explanation: Murakami, Hirose and colleagues found this transition in 2004 at conditions about 2,700 km down. The phase is 1.0–1.2% denser and may also explain strong anisotropy in D″.

prompt: Match each hypothesis for the LLSVPs to its central idea:

pairs.right: Clusters of hot upwellings blurred by tomography
Dense basaltic crust peeled off slabs piles up
Leftovers of early differentiation, such as a basal magma ocean
Buried relics of the Moon-forming impactor's mantle

explanation: Only the thermal model treats the provinces as hot ordinary mantle. The other three make them chemically distinct, differing in when and how the dense material got there.

prompt: Two 2017 studies reached different conclusions about the density of the LLSVPs. Which statement is correct?
options: Body-tide data suggested they are denser; Stoneley modes suggested they are less dense overall
Both found them about 10% denser than the surrounding mantle
Body-tide data suggested they are less dense; Stoneley modes suggested they are denser
Neither study could detect any density difference
correctAnswer: Body-tide data suggested they are denser; Stoneley modes suggested they are less dense overall
explanation: Lau and colleagues found the bottom two-thirds about 0.5% denser; Koelemeijer, Deuss and Ritsema found them less dense overall but could not rule out a dense layer about 100 km thick at the base.

prompt: The sharp margins of the LLSVPs, where shear-wave speed changes by several per cent over less than 100 km, are taken as a hint that they differ in composition.
explanation: Heat diffuses and blurs boundaries, so sharp walls suggest chemistry. The hint is not proof: some simulations with strongly temperature-dependent viscosity also produce sharp thermal edges.

prompt: Find the error in this description of ultra-low velocity zones:
steps: ULVZs are patches only tens of kilometres thick on the core–mantle boundary.
In them, S-wave speeds drop by up to 30% and P-wave speeds by up to 10%.
Seismic models fit them best with densities lower than the surrounding mantle.
Many lie beneath and along the margins of the LLSVPs.
Partial melt, very iron-rich ferropericlase or both could explain them.
explanation: Step 3 is wrong: ULVZs are best modelled with density increases of up to 10%. That is one reason very iron-rich material is a candidate alongside partial melt.

prompt: Put the steps of the 2023 Theia hypothesis for the LLSVPs in order:
steps: Theia strikes the proto-Earth in the giant impact that forms the Moon
Part of Theia's dense, iron-rich mantle ends up in the young Earth's solid lower mantle
Dense blobs of Theia material sink through the mantle
They gather into thermochemical piles above the core
The piles survive about 4.5 billion years of convection and are imaged as LLSVPs
explanation: Yuan and colleagues estimated Theia's mantle to be 2.0–3.5% denser than Earth's, enough to sink, pile up and survive. The idea is elegant but untested.

prompt: Who proposed in 1963 that the Hawaiian chain formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a stationary hotspot?
options: J. Tuzo Wilson
W. Jason Morgan
Harold Jeffreys
Gillian Foulger
explanation: Wilson's hotspot idea came in 1963. Morgan added deep mantle plumes as the source in 1971, and Foulger later championed the shallow Plate model as an alternative.

prompt: Wilson's hotspot idea predicts that volcanoes get older with distance from the active hotspot.
explanation: Plate motion carries each volcano away from the hotspot. In Hawaii the oldest rocks on Kauai are about 5.5 million years old, while the Big Island's are less than 0.7 million years old.

prompt: In 1971 W. Jason Morgan proposed that hotspots are fed by columns of hot rock rising from the deep mantle, called mantle _____.
explanation: Morgan's paper "Convection Plumes in the Lower Mantle" also showed that three Pacific island chains fit a rigid plate rotating over three fixed hotspots.

prompt: Match each study or model to its key claim:

pairs.right: At least six plumes reach the lowermost mantle
Broad conduits rooted in large ULVZs
The Hawaiian hotspot moved south at 4–5 cm per year
Melting anomalies come from shallow extension

explanation: The first two are imaging results for deep plumes; the drilling result undermines hotspot fixity; the Plate model rejects deep plumes as the general explanation.

prompt: Why did Ocean Drilling Program Leg 197 weaken the idea of fixed hotspots?
options: The latitudes at which Emperor Seamount lavas formed changed with age
It found no volcanic rock in the Emperor Seamounts
It showed the Pacific Plate has not moved
It found Kauai to be younger than the Big Island
correctAnswer: The latitudes at which Emperor Seamount lavas formed changed with age
explanation: Magnetism frozen into the lavas records the latitude where they formed. The trend shows the Hawaiian hotspot itself moved south at 4–5 cm per year between about 81 and 47 million years ago.

prompt: French and Romanowicz found that the conduits beneath major hotspots are narrower than classic thermal plume tails.
explanation: The conduits are broader than thermal plume tails, which suggests they are long-lived and perhaps thermochemical. They extend from the core–mantle boundary to about 1,000 km depth.

prompt: Put the life of a hotspot volcano in Wilson's model in order:
steps: Magma from the hotspot erupts on the sea floor as a seamount
The seamount grows until it emerges as an island volcano
Plate motion carries the volcano off the hotspot
Its volcanism ceases and it erodes as it ages
A new volcano grows over the hotspot behind it
explanation: Repeating this cycle builds a chain that ages steadily away from the hotspot, the age progression seen along the Hawaiian islands.

prompt: Which statement best summarises the plume debate today?
options: Some hotspots appear to be fed by deep plumes, while others probably are not
Every hotspot is a fixed, deep plume rising from the core–mantle boundary
No deep plume has ever been imaged
Hotspots are shallow everywhere, as fixed hotspots require
correctAnswer: Some hotspots appear to be fed by deep plumes, while others probably are not
explanation: Tomography shows deep conduits beneath Hawaii, Iceland, Samoa and others, but also plumes confined to the upper mantle, and drilling shows hotspots can drift. Neither side has won outright.

prompt: Where is the Earth's magnetic field generated?
options: In the liquid iron outer core, by a dynamo
In the solid inner core, which acts as a permanent magnet
In magnetic rocks of the crust
In the mantle transition zone
correctAnswer: In the liquid iron outer core, by a dynamo
explanation: Iron loses its magnetism at core temperatures, so no permanent magnet can do it. Flowing, electrically conducting liquid iron regenerates the field, as Elsasser proposed in 1946.

prompt: Glatzmaier and Roberts's 1995 computer simulation of the geodynamo produced a reversal of the magnetic dipole.
explanation: Their model maintained a field for over 40,000 simulated years, went through several excursions and then completed a reversal that shared some features with real ones.

prompt: When iron freezes onto the inner core it rejects light elements, and the rising buoyant liquid drives _____ convection.
explanation: Compositional (chemical) convection is one of the core's three power sources, with secular cooling and latent heat. It is why the inner core matters so much to the dynamo.

prompt: Match each study to its result:

pairs.right: Conductivity two to three times higher than assumed
Inner core less than 0.7 billion years old
Conductivity of 18–44 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹
Field strength rises 1–1.5 billion years ago

explanation: Calculations and one experiment pointed to high conductivity and a young inner core; a direct measurement found low conductivity; and the palaeointensity record suggested inner-core nucleation in the Mesoproterozoic.

prompt: Why does a higher thermal conductivity make the geodynamo harder to power?
options: More heat is conducted along the adiabat, leaving less to drive convection
It makes the whole core freeze solid
It stops the inner core rejecting light elements
It makes iron lose its electrical conductivity
correctAnswer: More heat is conducted along the adiabat, leaving less to drive convection
explanation: Only heat flow beyond the conducted amount can drive thermal convection. Pozzo and colleagues' values put the adiabatic heat flux at 15–16 terawatts, more than the mantle was thought to extract.

prompt: The Ediacaran Sept-Îles rocks record a magnetic field more than ten times stronger than today's.
explanation: They record the weakest field yet reported from such rocks, more than ten times weaker than today's, with scattered directions. Bono and colleagues read it as a faltering dynamo just before inner-core growth began.

prompt: Find the error in this account of the inner-core nucleation paradox:
steps: A liquid must be supercooled below its melting point before crystals form spontaneously.
Classical nucleation theory says the core needed several hundred kelvin of supercooling.
The core's present-day temperature easily allows that much supercooling.
So, on this theory, the inner core should not have formed.
Researchers are testing compositions, such as iron with 10–15% carbon, that may ease the problem.
explanation: Step 3 is wrong: the required supercooling is incompatible with estimates of the core's present-day temperature. That conflict is the paradox, and it is why compositions such as iron with carbon are being tested.

prompt: What did Borlina, Weiss and colleagues conclude in 2020 about the Jack Hills zircons?
options: Most are poor recorders magnetised later, so a dynamo before 3.5 billion years ago is unproven
They prove a strong field 4.2 billion years ago
They show the inner core formed 4 billion years ago
They show the field was stronger 4 billion years ago than today
correctAnswer: Most are poor recorders magnetised later, so a dynamo before 3.5 billion years ago is unproven
explanation: Tarduno's group had reported fields in zircons up to 4.2 billion years old. Borlina and colleagues found secondary magnetisation in most grains; Tarduno's group replied with new evidence for a primary record.

prompt: Why are earthquake doublets useful for studying the inner core?
options: Repeated waves along nearly the same path reveal changes in the inner core over time
They measure each earthquake's magnitude twice
They locate the Moho precisely
They show where hotspots are
correctAnswer: Repeated waves along nearly the same path reveal changes in the inner core over time
explanation: If nothing in the inner core changed, the two seismograms would match. Differences between them reveal rotation or changes near the inner core's surface.

prompt: When seismologists say the inner core sub-rotated from 2008 to 2023, they mean it stopped spinning.
explanation: The inner core turns with the Earth once a day. Sub-rotation means it lagged slightly behind the mantle; the measurements track only its tiny lead or lag.

prompt: In the inner core, P-waves travelling parallel to the spin axis are faster than those crossing the equatorial plane. This direction dependence is called _____.
explanation: Inner-core anisotropy was found in 1986 and is usually explained by partly aligned iron crystals. Song and Richards tracked rotation by following its symmetry axis.

prompt: Match each study to its conclusion about the inner core:

pairs.right: About 1° per year faster than the mantle
Rotation paused, part of a seven-decade oscillation
Six-year oscillation from nuclear test pairs
Rotation plus changes in the shallow inner core

explanation: Rate estimates shrank from 1° per year to about 0.05–0.15° per year, and studies now disagree over the period of the oscillation and over how much of the signal comes from the inner core's surface.

prompt: How did Phạm and Tkalčić probe the Earth's centre in 2023?
options: By stacking waveforms to detect waves bouncing along the Earth's diameter up to five times
By measuring the body tide with GPS
By dating zircon crystals
By drilling ice cores in Antarctica
correctAnswer: By stacking waveforms to detect waves bouncing along the Earth's diameter up to five times
explanation: Stacking many stations' records for single large earthquakes, such as the 2017 Solomon Islands earthquake, brought out repeated passes through the inner core and favoured an innermost ball about 650 km in radius.

prompt: Ishii and Dziewoński's innermost inner core and Phạm and Tkalčić's innermost ball have the same estimated radius.
explanation: Ishii and Dziewoński proposed a radius of about 300 km; Phạm and Tkalčić favoured about 650 km. Both find a distinct centre, but the sparse data leave its size uncertain.

prompt: Put the logic of the 2024 waveform-reversal study in order:
steps: Record inner-core waves from repeating earthquakes at the same arrays
Find that waveforms change between earlier and later events
Find later events whose waveforms change back to match earlier ones
Infer that the inner core has returned to an earlier position relative to the mantle
Chain the matches to reconstruct forward and backward motion over time
explanation: Wang, Vidale and colleagues used 143 pairs from 121 South Sandwich Islands earthquakes to show super-rotation from 2003 to 2008 and slower sub-rotation back along the same path from 2008 to 2023.

prompt: Find the error in this account of the 2025 study by Vidale's group:
steps: Yellowknife's rays graze the top of the inner core, while Eielson's dive deeper.
Between 2004 and 2008, extra changes appeared at Yellowknife but not at Eielson.
These changes appeared even when the inner core had returned to the same position, so rotation cannot explain them.
So the extra changes must come from the deepest part of the inner core.
Rotation and local change near the inner-core boundary are therefore both at work.
explanation: Step 4 is wrong. Because only the grazing Yellowknife paths changed, the extra changes point to the shallow inner core, most likely viscous deformation of the inner-core boundary.
